questions.question: What does `type Name = String` actually create?
options: A new type distinct from String
Another name for the existing String type
A subtype of String with extra restrictions
A type class that String must implement
questions.explanation: type introduces a synonym: another name for a type that already exists. Name and String are completely interchangeable everywhere, because GHC expands Name to String before it does anything else.
optionFeedback: That is what data creates (next lesson). type only renames — it never introduces a new, distinct type.
Correct — Name is simply another spelling of String. Every value of type Name is a String and vice versa.
Synonyms carry no restrictions of any kind; they are expanded away completely before type checking, so nothing about String is narrowed.
Type classes are a separate mechanism (Chapter 9); type introduces no class or instance at all.

questions.question: Given `type Age = Int`, is `birthdayOf :: Age -> Age` a different function from `birthdayOf :: Int -> Int`?
options: Yes, they accept different sets of values
No — Age and Int are the same type to the compiler, so the two signatures describe exactly the same function
Only if Age is also given a deriving clause
Yes, because Age is more restrictive
questions.explanation: A synonym adds no restriction and creates no new type. Age -> Age and Int -> Int are literally the same type after GHC expands the synonym, so any function with one signature could equally be written with the other.
optionFeedback: They accept exactly the same values — every Int is an Age and every Age is an Int, since they are the same type under a different name.
Correct — GHC expands Age to Int before checking anything, so the two signatures are indistinguishable to the compiler.
type synonyms cannot carry a deriving clause at all; that is only available on data and newtype declarations.
A synonym adds no restriction whatsoever — it is exactly as permissive as the type it renames.

questions.question: Why does `passed :: ClassList -> [Name]` typecheck against a list comprehension using `(n, m) <- cs`?
options: Because ClassList happens to coincide with Name
Because ClassList expands to [(Name, Mark)], so pattern matching (n, m) against each element is exactly the same as matching a [(String, Int)]
Because type synonyms allow pattern matching that other types forbid
It does not typecheck; the example is simplified
questions.explanation: ClassList = [Student] = [(Name, Mark)] = [(String, Int)] once every synonym is expanded. A list comprehension over cs :: ClassList is therefore identical, to the type checker, to one over a [(String, Int)] — the synonyms only change what a person reads.
optionFeedback: ClassList and Name are unrelated synonyms for different things ([( Name, Mark)] versus String) — this is not why the match works.
Correct — expanding every synonym gives [(String, Int)], and (n, m) destructures a pair exactly as it always would, synonym or not.
Synonyms grant no special pattern-matching privileges; matching works because of what the type expands to, not because of the synonym itself.
The example typechecks as written and runs exactly as shown in the transcript.

questions.question: `distance + height` typechecks even though `distance :: Metres` and `height :: Feet`. Why?
options: Haskell allows mixing any two numeric types
Metres and Feet both expand to Double before type checking, so both operands really are Double
+ is overloaded to convert automatically between units
It is a bug in this particular example only
questions.explanation: type introduces a name, not a boundary. Once GHC expands Metres and Feet, both distance and height are Double, and Double + Double is unremarkable — there is nothing left in the types to say they represented different units.
optionFeedback: Haskell is strict about mixing distinct numeric types (e.g. Int and Double do not add directly) — this example passes only because Metres and Feet are not distinct types at all.
Correct — after expansion, both sides of + are plain Double, so the addition is completely ordinary and unremarkable to the type checker.
+ knows nothing about units; there is no unit information left in the type once the synonyms are expanded away.
This is not a bug — it is the defining, predictable behaviour of type synonyms: no boundary is ever enforced.

questions.question: Which change would make `distance + height` a compile error, while keeping the values 100 and 30?
options: Renaming Metres to Metres2
Declaring Metres and Feet with newtype or data instead of type
Adding a comment explaining the units
Writing distance + height as (+) distance height
questions.explanation: Only newtype or data create a genuinely distinct type that the compiler tracks and refuses to mix. Renaming a synonym, writing a comment, or using prefix-operator syntax all leave the underlying representation — and the lack of protection — exactly the same.
optionFeedback: Renaming the synonym changes nothing about its behaviour; Metres2 would still expand straight to Double.
Correct — newtype or data make Metres and Feet genuinely separate types, so GHC rejects the addition at compile time, the next lesson's topic.
Comments carry no meaning to the type checker; they help a human reader but change nothing about what typechecks.
(+) distance height and distance + height are the exact same expression, just written prefix instead of infix — no behavioural difference.

questions.question: In `type Assoc k v = [(k, v)]`, what are `k` and `v`?
options: Concrete types, fixed once and for all
Type variables — placeholders that stand for whatever types are supplied when Assoc is used
Function names
Data constructors
questions.explanation: Lowercase names after a synonym's own name are type variables, exactly as in a polymorphic function signature (Chapter 9). Assoc String Int, Assoc Int Bool, and so on are all valid instantiations of the same parameterised synonym.
optionFeedback: Concrete types are capitalised, like Int or String. k and v are lowercase, marking them as variables, not fixed types.
Correct — k and v are type variables. Assoc is only a complete type once they are both supplied, e.g. Assoc String Int.
Function names are also lowercase, but k and v appear in a type declaration, not bound to any expression — they name type parameters.
Data constructors are capitalised values (Chapter 8's next lesson); k and v name types, not values.

questions.question: Why can `swapPair` be applied to `(1, 2) :: Pair Int` and also to `("left", "right") :: Pair String`?
options: swapPair has two separate definitions, one per type
Pair a is polymorphic in a, so swapPair :: Pair a -> Pair a works for any type a supplies
Int and String are secretly the same type
swapPair converts everything to String internally
questions.explanation: Pair a = (a, a) is parameterised: a is instantiated separately at each use. swapPair's signature, Pair a -> Pair a, is exactly as general as (a, a) -> (a, a), which places no constraint on what a is, so it works for Int, String, or any other type.
optionFeedback: Only one definition of swapPair was written; it works polymorphically rather than by overloading per type.
Correct — a is a type variable, instantiated to Int in one call and String in another, exactly as with any polymorphic function.
Int and String remain completely distinct types; swapPair simply does not care which one it is given, because it never inspects it beyond swapping positions.
swapPair only swaps the two positions of the tuple — it performs no conversion of any kind.
